items.title: Can exercise affect immune function to increase susceptibility to infection?
items.summary: This debate article examined the longstanding question of whether exercise itself can suppress immune function and increase susceptibility to infection. The paper pitted opposing arguments against each other on several contested issues, including whether high-performance athletes are genuinely more infection-prone than the general population, and whether exercise independently drives increased infection risk or whether confounding factors such as sleep disruption, psychological stress, travel, and nutritional deficits are responsible. While there is broad agreement that regular moderate-intensity exercise benefits immune defense—particularly in older adults and those with chronic disease—the picture is more complex for arduous exercise practiced by elite athletes and military personnel, who show high infection burdens. Both sides agreed that infection susceptibility is multifactorial in origin, but whether exercise itself is a causative factor remains unresolved, as does the reliability of biomarkers and the interpretation of existing in vitro and in vivo evidence. The authors conclude that more rigorous empirical research is needed to disentangle the independent contribution of exercise from the many co-occurring factors that characterize high-performance athletic environments.
items.citation: Richard J. Simpson, Richard J. Simpson, Maree Gleeson et al.. Can exercise affect immune function to increase susceptibility to infection?. PubMed. 2026

items.title: Spinal cord injury: Known and possible influences on the immune response to exercise
items.summary: This review paper examined how spinal cord injury affects immune function, with particular focus on the immune response to exercise. The authors conducted a comprehensive literature search to gather existing studies on exercise immunology across patient, recreationally active, and athlete populations with spinal cord injury. A central theme is that autonomic dysfunction following spinal cord injury alters resting and post-exercise catecholamine concentrations, which may directly suppress immune cells given that the vast majority of lymphoid cells express adrenergic receptors, with this effect being especially pronounced in individuals with tetraplegia. However, the review notes that some immune responses to exercise, such as increased natural killer cell cytotoxicity and mucosal immunity in those with tetraplegia, appear to operate independently of catecholamine changes, suggesting compensatory mechanisms such as sympathetic reflex activity, receptor hypersensitivity, or neuroendocrine adjustments may offset disability-related immune deficits. The authors conclude that exercise and rehabilitation can enhance certain measures of immunity and autonomic function following spinal cord injury, and call for further research to clarify the precise mechanisms involved and to leverage exercise as a tool for improving health in this population.
items.citation: Christof A. Leicht, Victoria Louise Goosey-Tolfrey, NICOLETTE CLAIRE BISHOP. Spinal cord injury: Known and possible influences on the immune response to exercise. PubMed. 2026

items.title: Understanding graft-versus-host disease. Preliminary findings regarding the effects of exercise in affected patients
items.summary: This paper examines graft-versus-host disease, a serious multi-systemic complication arising from allogeneic hematopoietic stem cell transplantation in which donor lymphocytes attack host tissues, with particular attention to its chronic form and its impact on patients' physical capacity. The authors conducted a review of the pathophysiological mechanisms underlying the disease alongside available evidence from both animal and human studies on the effects of exercise in affected individuals. Their findings suggest that exercise training as an adjunct therapy holds promise for improving physical fitness, potentially enhancing immune function, and reducing fatigue in this population, though the evidence base remains limited and the authors call for more randomized controlled trials specifically targeting patients with graft-versus-host disease.
items.citation: Carmen Fiuza‐Luces, Nuria Garatachea, Nathan A. Berger et al.. Understanding graft-versus-host disease. Preliminary findings regarding the effects of exercise in affected patients. PubMed. 2026

items.title: EHA Guidelines on management of chronic lymphocytic leukemia and Richter transformation
items.summary: This paper presents updated European guidelines for the management of chronic lymphocytic leukemia and, for the first time, Richter transformation. The guidelines were developed under the European Hematology Association, which assumes sole responsibility for future editions and commits to annual updates to reflect the rapidly evolving landscape of research and clinical practice. A consensus process among experts from multiple European countries was used, and notably included patient advocacy representatives for the first time in line with standard procedures. The guidelines advocate a holistic approach to disease management spanning initial diagnosis and active surveillance through treatment decisions informed by both disease- and patient-specific factors. Key treatment updates include the newly approved time-limited combination of acalabrutinib and venetoclax with or without obinutuzumab as a first-line option, as well as continuous pirtobrutinib for patients who have been exposed to covalent Bruton's tyrosine kinase inhibitors in the relapsed or refractory setting.
items.citation: Barbara F. Eichhorst, Paolo Ghia, Francesc Bosch et al.. EHA Guidelines on management of chronic lymphocytic leukemia and Richter transformation. HemaSphere. 2026

items.title: Accelerating protein design by scaling experimental characterization
items.summary: This paper addresses the bottleneck of experimental validation in de novo protein design, where computational methods for generating new protein sequences have far outpaced the capacity to test them biochemically. The authors developed Semi-Automated Protein Production, a rapid, modular, and cost-effective workflow combining experimental and computational steps to enable milligram-scale protein production and standardized characterization of hundreds of designs per day using mostly standard laboratory equipment, with full end-to-end execution in roughly two days. To further reduce costs, they also developed a complementary demultiplexing protocol that uses pooled synthetic oligonucleotides as input DNA, dramatically lowering the per-construct expense and enabling thousands of designs to be purified and characterized in arrayed format. The platform was validated by applying it to rapidly characterize computationally designed inhibitors of respiratory syncytial virus, demonstrating its utility across a wide range of real design projects. The authors argue that by using partial automation rather than complex end-to-end robotics, these protocols are broadly adoptable and could substantially accelerate the protein design field.
items.citation: Jason Qian, Lukas F. Milles, Basile I. M. Wicky et al.. Accelerating protein design by scaling experimental characterization. Nature Communications. 2026

items.title: Human lung organoid modelling of tissue-resident antiviral T cell responses
items.summary: This paper investigated tissue-resident immune responses in the human lung, particularly the question of whether memory T cell responses to respiratory pathogens can occur autonomously within lung tissue without input from secondary lymphoid organs. The researchers developed long-term adult human distal lung organoids derived from intact tissue fragments, cultured in a three-dimensional air-liquid interface system that preserved both the epithelial and stromal architecture as well as endogenous lung-resident immune cells including T, B, NK, and myeloid cells. The organoid T cells maintained residency and memory markers, sustained cytokine-assisted persistence, and retained T cell receptor repertoires matching those of fresh donor tissue. When the organoids were infected with SARS-CoV-2, the virus productively infected the lung epithelium, triggered inflammatory cytokine responses, and elicited virus-specific tissue-resident T cell responses within the organoid system. These findings demonstrate that the lung possesses organ-autonomous capacity for antigen-specific memory T cell recall, independent of secondary lymphoid tissue, and establish this organoid platform as a tool for studying tissue-resident immunity in human lung disease.
items.citation: Joseph K. Rathkey, S. S. Choi, Vincent van Unen et al.. Human lung organoid modelling of tissue-resident antiviral T cell responses. Nature. 2026

items.title: SciCheck: A Framework for Verifying the Integrity of Deep Learning Training
items.summary: This paper addresses the challenge of verifying the integrity of deep learning training within scientific workflows, where non-determinism and flexible configurations make straightforward replication impossible as a validity check. The authors developed SciCheck, a framework that uses a provenance ledger to record training blueprints and evaluates runs through two complementary mechanisms: a statistical judge that compares per-step gradient statistics against a reference run, and a spot-check that re-executes randomly selected training segments anchored by committed checkpoints. The system was tested across multiple neural network architectures and against adversarial scenarios including gradient sign flipping, label poisoning, and fully fabricated runs, achieving high integrity detection while rejecting very few honest runs. The authors formally characterize the detection capabilities of each layer, showing that gradient statistics alone can catch sufficiently severe sign flips but are blind to fabricated runs that replay genuine statistics, while the spot-check provides probabilistic soundness guarantees that scale predictably with the number of sampled segments. Overall, the framework achieves strong verification performance at modest computational overhead relative to a single retraining, with efficient checkpoint storage through per-epoch commitments.
items.citation: Alexander Nguyen, Dylan Gresham, Gaby G. Dagher et al.. SciCheck: A Framework for Verifying the Integrity of Deep Learning Training. arXiv. 2026

items.title: Scenario Orchestration for Closed-loop Policy Evaluation of Autonomous Driving
items.summary: This paper addresses a fundamental challenge in autonomous driving evaluation: when a scripted test scenario is run in closed loop, the ego vehicle's responses can invalidate the intended interactions, making it difficult to assess policy behavior under specific conditions. The authors developed a scenario orchestrator that continuously monitors the full traffic state and dynamically adjusts non-ego actors through re-timing, re-routing, and role reassignment to preserve a desired scenario intent as the ego vehicle behaves unexpectedly. At each timestep, the system solves a constrained optimization problem that balances maintaining the intended interaction against minimizing interventions and preserving traffic plausibility. The approach also separates the question of whether a scenario was successfully realized from whether the ego policy handled it correctly, enabling more principled evaluation. Experiments in the CARLA simulator demonstrate that orchestration produces the targeted interactions more reliably than fixed scripted scenarios or learned reactive actor baselines, especially under varied initial conditions and diverse ego policies.
items.citation: Frieda Rong, Zhaoyue Wang, Veer Kapadia et al.. Scenario Orchestration for Closed-loop Policy Evaluation of Autonomous Driving. arXiv. 2026

items.title: An Empirical Study on Clustering-based Quantum Approximate Optimization Algorithm for Regression Test Case Selection
items.summary: The paper investigates the use of a clustering-based Quantum Approximate Optimization Algorithm (QAOA-TCS) for the problem of regression test case selection, which seeks to identify which tests to re-run after software modifications without executing the full test suite. The authors conducted an empirical evaluation comparing QAOA-TCS against both classical approaches and other quantum methods across single- and multi-objective formulations, also testing its robustness under varying levels of quantum noise. In the multi-objective setting, QAOA-TCS outperformed state-of-the-art competitors in most cases and remained stable even at high noise levels, while in the single-objective setting, QAOA-based methods performed comparably to one another. Regarding efficiency, a prior quantum annealing method proved most efficient for large multi-objective problems, whereas QAOA-TCS offered the best effectiveness-efficiency trade-off in the single-objective case on noisy simulators. The authors note that comparisons are limited by the different computational environments required to run the various algorithms.

items.title: Detection of Chagas disease from the ECG: the George B. Moody PhysioNet Challenge 2025
items.summary: The paper describes a competition challenge aimed at detecting Chagas disease, a parasitic infection causing cardiomyopathy, using electrocardiogram recordings as a non-invasive screening tool. Researchers organized a large-scale open challenge using over three hundred sixty thousand ECGs from multiple Brazilian databases, incorporating both weakly labeled data from patient reports and strongly labeled data from serological testing, alongside data augmentation strategies to improve model generalizability. The challenge framed detection as a triage task using a metric that measured the true positive rate among the patients most likely to have Chagas disease, calibrated to reflect realistic local serological testing capacity. Teams developed a wide range of algorithmic approaches, and the organizers additionally built an ensemble model combining the top submissions to improve and stabilize performance across datasets. The results demonstrated that ECG-based screening can achieve clinically meaningful sensitivity for prioritizing patients for Chagas disease testing, with the ensemble approach showing more consistent performance across datasets than any single model alone.
items.citation: Matthew A. Reyna, Soheil Saghafi, Zuzana Koscova et al.. Detection of Chagas disease from the ECG: the George B. Moody PhysioNet Challenge 2025. Physiological Measurement. 2026

items.title: Continuous wavelet-based feature extraction for laser-induced breakdown spectroscopy classification of human plasma samples
items.summary: This study investigated whether continuous wavelet transform-based feature extraction from laser-induced breakdown spectroscopy spectra could distinguish between human plasma samples from individuals who tested positive or negative for SARS-CoV-2. Dried plasma droplets on silicon substrates were analyzed using a nanosecond laser, with multiple single-shot measurements averaged per specimen after outlier rejection, and the extracted spectral peaks were fed into a support vector machine classifier. The wavelet-based pipeline identified emission lines associated with calcium, potassium, and nitrogen as discriminative features between the two groups. Leave-one-out cross-validation yielded high accuracy, sensitivity, and specificity, though the authors note these estimates are provisional and require reconciliation at the specimen-prediction level. The authors conclude that while the workflow offers a basis for examining spectral differences between the plasma groups, independent validation and assessment of sources of variability are necessary before any diagnostic relevance can be established.
items.citation: Md Mahmudur Rahman, Atqiya Munawara Mahi, Nazim Ahmed Belabbaci et al.. Continuous wavelet-based feature extraction for laser-induced breakdown spectroscopy classification of human plasma samples. arXiv. 2026

items.title: Advances in tuberculosis diagnostics and biomarkers, 2020-26: scientific evidence, recommendations, gaps, and developmental priorities.
items.summary: This paper reviews advances in tuberculosis diagnostics and biomarker research over roughly a five-year period, synthesizing evidence that has informed updated WHO policy guidance consolidating recommendations for detecting tuberculosis disease and drug resistance into a single framework. Key developments include the expanded role of digital chest radiography with computer-aided detection as a frontline screening and triage tool, and the broader decentralized deployment of rapid molecular diagnostics—including low-complexity automated and manual nucleic acid amplification tests—across diverse specimen types such as stool, gastric aspirate, nasopharyngeal samples, and tongue swabs, improving bacteriological confirmation especially in children and sputum-scarce populations. Drug-resistance testing has progressed through newer molecular platforms and the endorsement of targeted next-generation sequencing at reference laboratory level, while urine lipoarabinomannan assays improve diagnostic yield in people with HIV with advanced disease but remain limited in broader application. Host blood transcriptomic signatures show promising short-term prognostic and triage performance, and multiple other biomarker classes are advancing through clinical evaluation, yet none has met WHO target product profile criteria for a point-of-care test that reliably distinguishes infection from disease—including subclinical tuberculosis. The paper concludes that substantial gaps in performance, implementation, and equity persist and identifies these as priority areas for further development.
items.citation: Walzl G, McHugh TD, Chakaya J et al.. Advances in tuberculosis diagnostics and biomarkers, 2020-26: scientific evidence, recommendations, gaps, and developmental priorities.. The Lancet. Microbe. 2027

items.title: Sample-to-answer automated centrifugal microfluidics with computer-vision readout for point-of-care molecular diagnostics
items.summary: This paper addressed the need for automated, decentralized diagnostic tools capable of handling infectious disease outbreaks without relying on centralized laboratories. The researchers developed a fully automated centrifugal microfluidic platform that integrates loop-mediated isothermal amplification with computer-vision-based optical readout, designed to operate from sample to answer at the press of a single button. The system was validated using SARS-CoV-2 detection as a model, processing multiple samples simultaneously in under an hour without user intervention. Testing with RNA fragments spiked into water and artificial saliva demonstrated consistent detection down to a low copy-number sensitivity per reaction. The authors propose that this platform architecture provides a generalizable template for rapid, point-of-care molecular diagnostics suited to future outbreak responses, particularly in resource-limited settings.
items.citation: Akhtar AS, Lapins N, Moura JM et al.. Sample-to-answer automated centrifugal microfluidics with computer-vision readout for point-of-care molecular diagnostics. 2026

items.title: Beyond blood: a narrative review of advancements in saliva-based diagnostics.
items.summary: This narrative review examines the potential of human whole saliva as a noninvasive diagnostic biofluid capable of reflecting both systemic and oral physiology as an alternative to conventional blood-based testing. The authors synthesized existing evidence on salivary biomarkers spanning glycemic control, cardiovascular risk, critical care, endocrinology, infectious disease, cancer liquid biopsy, and neurodegenerative disorders, while also evaluating the analytical technologies used to detect them, from immunoassays and mass spectrometry to wearable electrochemical biosensors. The review further distinguished between regulatory-cleared diagnostic platforms and those still in the discovery phase. Despite considerable promise, the authors identify key barriers to clinical translation, including unstandardized collection protocols, interference from the oral matrix, and the absence of validated normative reference intervals. They conclude that mainstream adoption will require universal sampling standardization, matrix-matched biosensor engineering capable of sub-picomolar detection, and rigorous multicenter prospective trials to establish clinical cutoffs and validate blood-saliva correlation dynamics.
items.citation: Mondal S, Das Sharma A, Mandal SK et al.. Beyond blood: a narrative review of advancements in saliva-based diagnostics.. Expert review of molecular diagnostics. 2026

items.title: Sequential diagnosis with language models
items.summary: The paper investigated whether frontier language models could replicate the iterative, stepwise nature of clinical reasoning, known as sequential diagnosis, in which a clinician progressively gathers information to narrow down a diagnosis. The researchers developed an interactive benchmark and an AI system designed to simulate a panel of physicians, which continuously updated a differential diagnosis and selected cost-effective diagnostic tests from a brief initial clinical presentation. When evaluated on two datasets—complex case records from a major medical journal and real-world emergency department admissions—the AI system substantially outperformed generalist physicians on diagnostic accuracy while operating within a framework that also considered workup cost. The authors acknowledge these results were obtained under controlled benchmark conditions but argue they demonstrate meaningful potential for language models to assist clinicians in achieving more accurate and resource-efficient diagnoses.
items.citation: Harsha Nori, Mayank Daswani, Christopher Kelly et al.. Sequential diagnosis with language models. Science. 2026

items.title: MedicalAgentsBench for complex medical reasoning: Comparing internalized reasoning models versus externalized agent-based frameworks
items.summary: This paper investigated whether internalized reasoning models and externalized agent-based frameworks represent competing or complementary approaches to complex medical reasoning in large language models. The authors constructed a curated benchmark of complex clinical questions drawn from eight medical datasets, using difficulty-aware filtering and contamination screening, then evaluated a broad range of internalized reasoning models, base models, and agent-based methods against it. They found that both approaches independently improve performance on complex clinical questions, and critically, that their benefits compound when combined, with the highest accuracy achieved by applying agent workflows on top of an internalized reasoning model. Pareto analysis confirmed that this hybrid combination dominates the cost-performance frontier, while lightweight optimization on less expensive models was identified as a viable strategy for resource-constrained settings. The findings suggest that internalized and externalized reasoning approaches are complementary rather than mutually exclusive for complex medical question answering.
items.citation: Yanjun Shao, Xiangru Tang, Jiwoong Sohn et al.. MedicalAgentsBench for complex medical reasoning: Comparing internalized reasoning models versus externalized agent-based frameworks. Patterns. 2026

items.title: A framework for developing university policies on generative AI governance: a cross-national comparative study
items.summary: This study examined how universities across different national contexts are developing policies to govern the use of generative artificial intelligence in higher education, focusing on institutions in the United States, Japan, and China. The researchers conducted a cross-national comparative analysis of existing generative AI guidelines from leading universities in these three countries, applying an extended Technology Acceptance Model as an analytical lens across five domains and identifying key themes through thematic coding. The analysis revealed distinct national policy orientations, with American universities emphasizing faculty autonomy and adaptability, Japanese universities prioritizing ethics and risk management in alignment with government direction, and Chinese universities reflecting a centralized model focused on technology application and integration. Drawing on these comparative findings, the researchers proposed the University Policy Development Framework for Generative AI, which integrates technological, organizational, and social dimensions to help institutions balance innovation against risk. The framework is intended to support universities in assessing policy priorities and building institutional capacity for sustainable generative AI governance.
items.citation: Ming Li, Qin Xie, Ariunaa Enkhtur et al.. A framework for developing university policies on generative AI governance: a cross-national comparative study. Studies in Higher Education. 2026

items.title: Multi-omics and artificial intelligence for precision drug discovery and potential clinical applications
items.summary: This review examines how the integration of multiomics technologies and artificial intelligence is reshaping precision drug discovery and clinical translation. The authors synthesize how genomic, transcriptomic, proteomic, and metabolomic approaches collectively illuminate disease mechanisms at the molecular level, while deep learning architectures enable the extraction of meaningful patterns from these complex, high-dimensional datasets. The paper analyzes the combined application of these technologies across the drug development pipeline, encompassing target identification, drug repositioning, de novo compound design, virtual screening, pharmacokinetic modeling, and safety assessment. Disease areas including oncology, neurodegeneration, and cardiovascular conditions are used to illustrate how this convergence supports more precise therapeutic interventions. The authors also acknowledge persistent challenges, including the harmonization of disparate omics data, reproducibility concerns, and the mitigation of algorithmic bias, while arguing that the fusion of multiomics and artificial intelligence heralds a new era in bench-to-clinic translational medicine.
items.citation: Yuqing Liu, Kun Zhu, Weijun Peng et al.. Multi-omics and artificial intelligence for precision drug discovery and potential clinical applications. Signal Transduction and Targeted Therapy. 2026

items.title: Health-System-Wide Mapping of Demographic Information in Routine Clinical Histopathology
items.summary: This paper investigated how much demographic information — specifically sex, age group, and self-reported race — is encoded within routine clinical histopathology slides across a broad range of organs and disease states. The researchers analyzed a very large collection of hematoxylin and eosin whole-slide images from hundreds of thousands of patients spanning twenty-five organs, applying pathology foundation-model representations combined with multiple-instance learning to systematically recover demographic attributes from tissue appearance. Demographic signals were broadly detectable across all three attributes and across organ types, with performance varying considerably by organ and demographic category. Importantly, demographic-associated signals persisted even after controlling for diagnosis-based groupings, suggesting these signals reflect genuine histomorphological and contextual variation rather than being entirely explained by disease composition or class imbalance. The authors argue that their findings provide a systematic map useful for understanding the biological and contextual sources of these signals, assessing risks of shortcut learning in computational pathology models, and guiding the development of more interpretable and equitable AI tools for pathology.
items.citation: Shengjia Chen, Ruchika Verma, Kevin Clare et al.. Health-System-Wide Mapping of Demographic Information in Routine Clinical Histopathology. arXiv. 2026

items.title: Fifty-Two Shades of Pig: What the UCR Archive Really Asks Classifiers to Do
items.summary: The paper investigates whether the UCR Time Series Classification Archive, which serves as the standard benchmark for time series classification research, actually reflects the kinds of problems the field intends to solve. The authors conducted a provenance audit of the archive's datasets, examining their original experimental contexts, construction methods, and evaluation splits. They found that multiple datasets have been repurposed from their original classification tasks into different ones, that some datasets originate from toy or artificial setups, and that certain test splits are flawed. The authors also raise concerns about how well ordered non-temporal sequences such as spectra and shape outlines represent genuine time series classification, and about potential issues introduced by decomposing multivariate problems. These findings call into question the validity of drawing broad conclusions about classifier performance from archive-wide benchmark scores and advocate for greater attention to evaluation conditions that reflect real deployment scenarios.
items.citation: Omar Swelam, Jaris Küken, Shi Bin Hoo et al.. Fifty-Two Shades of Pig: What the UCR Archive Really Asks Classifiers to Do. arXiv. 2026

items.title: Seeing What Matters: Benchmarking Task-Conditioned Actionable Spatial Belief for Manipulation
items.summary: This paper addresses the problem of task-conditioned visual information gathering for robot manipulation, asking whether a model can identify which views of a scene are actually useful for executing a specific command rather than merely describing the scene in general. The authors introduce a benchmark called Seeing What Matters, built across three simulated tabletop manipulation domains, that pairs candidate camera views with manipulation commands and evaluates whether a view-selection policy acquires the observations needed to make that command executable. The benchmark includes hundreds of frozen evaluation cases that expand to over a hundred thousand evaluator episodes under two protocols measuring closed-loop actionability and out-of-distribution functional generalization. A diagnostic reference pipeline that maintains a spatial-functional belief state and prioritizes views by missing evidence achieves near-perfect success, while ablating its functional or command-binding components collapses performance to near zero, and seven vision-language models tested on the same cases reach only a fraction of that performance. The authors conclude that spatial belief for manipulation should be evaluated by whether it acquires task-relevant evidence rather than by general scene completeness.
items.citation: Yina Jian, Mingkun Xu. Seeing What Matters: Benchmarking Task-Conditioned Actionable Spatial Belief for Manipulation. arXiv. 2026

items.title: Probing injection locking of an integrated nanolaser pair through RF beating
items.summary: This paper investigated simultaneous optical injection locking of a pair of photonic-crystal nanolasers integrated onto a common silicon waveguide and coupled to a single master laser. Because fabrication-induced disorder caused the two nanolasers to emit at slightly different wavelengths, their individual locking ranges could be distinguished and characterized as a function of master laser detuning and power. The researchers identified a regime where both nanolasers locked simultaneously to the master laser, and they probed this collective state by modulating each nanolaser independently at distinct radio frequencies. A beat note at the difference of these modulation frequencies emerged exclusively within the region of simultaneous locking, serving as a clear radio-frequency signature of the shared locked state. The work establishes RF beating as a practical and compact diagnostic tool for characterizing common-master injection locking in integrated nanolaser systems.
items.citation: Jan-Niklas Topf, Roberto Gajardo, Guillaume Huyet et al.. Probing injection locking of an integrated nanolaser pair through RF beating. arXiv. 2026

items.title: Local Correlations Determine the Dephasing Threshold of $\mathbb{Z}_2$ Topology
items.summary: The paper investigates how dephasing noise affects the survival of band topology in the Kane-Mele topological insulator, which carries a symmetry-protected topological invariant. To determine the stability of this invariant under dephasing, the authors construct an auxiliary single-particle correlation Hamiltonian that reproduces the single-particle correlations of the open quantum system exactly. They find that the transition from topological to trivial phase is signaled by the closing of a gap in this correlation Hamiltonian, which is linked to the purity gap of the mixed state. As complementary diagnostics, they compute the topological invariant directly and demonstrate quantized conductance in two-terminal transport through the auxiliary Hamiltonian in the nontrivial phase, while clarifying that this does not imply physical conductance under dephasing. The central result is a predictive, local criterion based on single-particle correlations that determines whether topological structure survives a given noise channel.
items.citation: Rishith Reddy, Ashutosh Dubey, Partha Sarathi et al.. Local Correlations Determine the Dephasing Threshold of $\mathbb{Z}_2$ Topology. arXiv. 2026

Through an interdisciplinary analysis, they assessed ethical, regulatory, and implementation considerations to support the development of target product profiles for dengue treatments by the WHO. Their findings emphasize the importance of enhanced surveillance to better characterize at-risk groups, co-produced research approaches that include these populations in trial design and care decisions, and strategies to overcome access barriers such as the lack of rapid diagnostics. The authors propose that this framework could serve as a broader model for equitable development and delivery of countermeasures against other infectious disease threats to global health.

items.title: Stone and water governed early human settlement of the desert
items.summary: This paper investigated why early human dispersals into desert environments like the Arabian Peninsula were geographically limited even during periods when water was available. Despite finding abundant evidence of ancient freshwater sources across dozens of localities with excellent ground visibility, they discovered a complete absence of stone artefacts and knappable raw materials throughout the survey area. Spatial modelling of the Arabian Peninsula demonstrated that settlement patterns were better explained by the simultaneous availability of water and knappable stone than by water alone, substantially improving the predictive accuracy of site location models. The authors argue that access to lithic raw materials functioned as an independent constraint on early human settlement alongside water availability, and that this principle holds across Africa, North America, and Asia, meaning that dispersal models relying solely on climate and hydrology likely overestimate the habitable range of stone-tool-dependent populations.
items.why_notable: This work is drawing attention because it challenges the assumption that water availability alone drove early human settlement in desert environments, revealing instead that access to suitable toolmaking stone was equally essential. Through a genome-wide CRISPR screen, the tetraspanin CD9 was identified as the host receptor for Delta toxin, and genetic ablation of CD9 in myeloid cells protected mice from toxin-induced lethality and multiorgan injury. The findings reframe a subset of NEC as a toxin-mediated disorder and establish the Delta toxin-CD9 axis as a therapeutic target, further supported by the protective efficacy of a neutralizing anti-Delta toxin monoclonal antibody.

By characterizing this pseudo-direct bandgap nature, they demonstrated that the material exhibits substantially slowed bimolecular electron–hole recombination compared to conventional direct-gap semiconductors, because charge carriers relax into the indirect valley where radiative recombination is suppressed. This decoupling of strong optical absorption from rapid emission represents a potential route to circumventing the thermodynamic limitations imposed by Planck's law, pointing toward new opportunities in solar energy conversion.

items.title: Perinatal elimination of genetically aberrant human cortical neurons
items.summary: This study investigated how the human brain manages neurons with abnormal genomes during development, focusing on somatic copy number variants arising in individual neurons. The researchers sequenced thousands of single neurons from human postmortem brain tissue spanning fetal to postnatal life using two distinct whole-genome sequencing approaches, supplemented by single-nucleus chromatin accessibility and RNA sequencing of tens of thousands of nuclei. They found that a substantial proportion of prenatal cortical neurons carry highly aberrant genomes characterized by widespread copy number variants affecting multiple chromosomes, but this proportion drops dramatically after birth in a pattern temporally aligned with known periods of programmed cell death. Neurons that survived into postnatal life showed depletion of copy number variants affecting dosage-sensitive genes and genes linked to neurodevelopmental disorders, and neurons bearing high copy number variant burdens displayed abnormal synaptic gene expression, implicating disrupted synaptic regulation in their elimination. The authors conclude that perinatal removal of genomically defective neurons represents a form of purifying selection and genome quality control during human neurodevelopment, a process that may be disrupted in neurodevelopmental disease.
items.why_notable: This work is attracting attention because it reveals that the developing human brain appears to have a quality-control mechanism that selectively eliminates neurons carrying widespread genomic abnormalities around the time of birth. The finding, based on single-neuron sequencing, suggests that what initially appears to be common prenatal genomic instability is largely pruned away during a critical perinatal window.
items.citation: Diane D. Shao, Yifan Zhao, Joseph Brew et al.. Perinatal elimination of genetically aberrant human cortical neurons. Nature. 2026

items.title: Subcycle videography of Landau–Zener–Majorana transitions in graphene
items.summary: This paper investigated the subcycle dynamics of electrons driven by strong light fields in graphene, focusing on the fundamental quantum process of Landau–Zener–Majorana interband tunnelling. The researchers developed an attosecond-precision band-structure videography technique capable of imaging electron distributions across the entire first Brillouin zone with subcycle temporal resolution, overcoming previous limitations that confined such measurements to small electron momenta. By applying this technique to graphene's Dirac-like band structure, they directly visualized how strong-field-driven electron acceleration combines with periodic non-adiabatic tunnelling events to produce coherent subcycle displacement and distortion of the carrier distribution at the Brillouin zone edge. The highly non-thermal electron distributions captured in these measurements additionally allowed competing scattering processes to be disentangled and their influence on coherent electronic control to be assessed. The approach provides a new level of microscopic insight into how strong light fields control quantum materials and opens possibilities for all-optical engineering of electron trajectories and phases of matter.
items.why_notable: This work draws attention because it demonstrates a technique capable of capturing electron dynamics with attosecond precision across an entire Brillouin zone, making it possible to directly visualize ultrafast quantum transitions in graphene driven by lightwaves at a subcycle timescale.
items.citation: Vincent Eggers, Giacomo Inzani, Manuel Meierhofer et al.. Subcycle videography of Landau–Zener–Majorana transitions in graphene. Nature. 2026

items.title: Diet at disease onset determines tissue inflammatory memory
items.summary: This study investigated whether brief dietary changes during acute inflammatory episodes can shape both immediate immune responses and long-term tissue memory, independent of chronic obesity. Using mouse models of skin and lung inflammation, the researchers exposed lean animals to a high-fat diet only during a narrow window surrounding disease onset, and found this transient exposure dramatically amplified inflammatory severity to levels seen in chronically obese animals. Mechanistically, the high-fat diet rapidly recruited neutrophils to inflamed tissue, where they expressed elevated levels of the NLRP3 inflammasome and IL-1β, and blocking this neutrophil–NLRP3–IL-1β axis through depletion, genetic deletion, or pharmacological inhibition was sufficient to prevent the dietary amplification of disease. Critically, even after recovery and return to a low-fat diet, a chromatin-poised population of tissue-resident memory T cells persisted, causing exaggerated inflammatory responses upon disease recurrence. These findings demonstrate that a transient physiological state coinciding with tissue inflammation can become durably embedded in local immune memory, fundamentally altering future disease trajectory.
items.why_notable: This work is attracting attention because it reveals that what an organism eats at the specific moment a disease begins can permanently alter how the disease progresses, suggesting that a brief dietary window has lasting consequences for tissue inflammation.
items.citation: Zewen Jiang, John M. Tayeri, Im‐Hong Sun et al.. Diet at disease onset determines tissue inflammatory memory. Nature. 2026

items.title: T and B cells recognize splicing-derived neutrophil neoantigens in lupus
items.summary: This paper investigated whether aberrant mRNA splicing in neutrophils from systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) patients generates novel peptide sequences capable of driving autoimmune responses. The researchers compared splicing patterns in neutrophils from SLE patients, healthy donors, and rheumatoid arthritis patients, identifying numerous mis-spliced transcripts unique to SLE that were predicted to encode novel amino acid sequences not found in any normal proteins. Using mass spectrometry, they confirmed that peptides derived from these aberrant sequences are presented on class I MHC molecules in patient samples, and functional assays demonstrated that patient T cells expanded and were reactivated by these peptides to produce inflammatory cytokines. Additionally, SLE patient serum contained IgG autoantibodies specifically recognizing epitopes within the novel sequences, particularly in patients predicted to harbor the corresponding cryptic splicing events. The study concludes that dysregulated mRNA splicing in SLE neutrophils produces neoantigens that have driven T and B cell activation, clonal expansion, class-switch recombination, and ultimately autoimmunity, drawing a parallel to neoantigen-driven anti-tumor immunity.
items.why_notable: This work is attracting attention because it identifies a mechanism by which aberrant RNA splicing in neutrophils produces novel peptides that drive the autoimmune responses characteristic of lupus, linking splicing-derived neoantigens to T cell activation and autoantibody production. The findings reframe lupus as potentially neoantigen-driven, opening new avenues for understanding and targeting the disease.
items.citation: Mohammed Saeed, Xiaoxing Wang, Farheen Shaikh et al.. T and B cells recognize splicing-derived neutrophil neoantigens in lupus. Nature. 2026

items.title: Rare and common genetic variants shape single-cell immune gene expression
items.summary: This study investigated how both common and rare genetic variants influence gene expression across immune cell types at single-cell resolution. The researchers generated and analyzed a large matched dataset combining whole-genome sequencing and single-cell RNA sequencing from nearly two thousand individuals, encompassing millions of cells across dozens of immune cell types, representing the first phase of the TenK10K project. Using a method that models individual cells directly rather than aggregated pseudobulk counts, they mapped expression quantitative trait loci in a cell type-specific manner, identifying putative common regulatory variants for the majority of genes tested and cumulative rare variant signals for nearly half of all genes. They found that approximately half of the detected genetic effects are specific to one or only a few cell types, and they further characterized how genetic variants influence gene expression across continuous cell states and affect cell state abundance. By integrating these findings with functional annotations and disease data, the study illuminates the molecular mechanisms underlying many disease-associated genetic variants and advances understanding of cell type-specific gene regulation.
items.why_notable: This work is attracting attention because it pairs single-cell RNA sequencing with whole-genome sequencing across thousands of individuals to reveal how both common and rare genetic variants influence gene expression in specific immune cell types—an angle that has been largely unexplored for rare variants. The scale and resolution of the dataset enable discovery of variant-expression associations that previous studies lacked the power to detect.
items.citation: Anna S. E. Cuomo, Eleanor Spenceley, Hope A. Tanudisastro et al.. Rare and common genetic variants shape single-cell immune gene expression. Nature. 2026

items.title: Emotion regulation capacity lacks a shared neural signature
items.summary: This paper investigated whether brain activity during cognitive reappraisal — a key emotion regulation strategy — provides a reliable neural signature of individual differences in reappraisal ability. Using a large consortium of neuroimaging datasets encompassing thousands of participants, the researchers examined associations between task-evoked neural activation and three common measures of reappraisal capability: trait questionnaires, task-based emotional ratings, and amygdala down-regulation. Strikingly, they found no meaningful overlap across these three indices, with only a negligible correlation between amygdala down-regulation and emotional ratings, and no reliable whole-brain neural correlates of trait reappraisal. Neural associations with emotional ratings appeared outside canonical prefrontal emotion regulation circuits, and amygdala down-regulation was confounded by idiosyncratic whole-brain response patterns. The authors conclude that trait, behavioral, and neural measures likely capture distinct facets of emotion regulation rather than a common construct, and they raise broader methodological concerns for neuroimaging research on individual differences in personality, psychopathology, and well-being.
items.why_notable: This work is attracting attention because it challenges the long-held assumption that prefrontal control circuits serve as the neural basis of emotion regulation capacity, instead pointing to sensorimotor and amygdala activation as the relevant indicators. The findings suggest that the brain's signature of how well people regulate their emotions is fundamentally different from what the field has canonically assumed.
items.citation: Maurizio Sicorello, Jenny Zähringer, Thomas E. Kraynak et al.. Emotion regulation capacity lacks a shared neural signature. Nature. 2026

items.title: Tumour assembloids recapitulate tumour–CAF–T cell crosstalk in renal cancer
items.summary: This study investigated how cancer cells, cancer-associated fibroblasts (CAFs), and immune cells interact within the renal cell carcinoma tumor microenvironment to influence responses to immunotherapy. The researchers developed combinatorial tumor assembloids by reconstituting multiple human renal cell carcinoma components in a mix-and-match fashion, and used genetically engineered versions of these assembloids alongside humanized mouse models to dissect cellular crosstalk. They discovered a tumor–CAF–T cell signaling axis in which tumor-derived WNT signals induce CAFs to express activin A, which in turn sustains CD8+ T cell stemness and enhances sensitivity to anti-PD-1 therapy. In patients who do not respond to treatment, a subset of WNT-unresponsive CAFs fails to produce activin A, resulting in impaired CD8+ T cell stemness and therapeutic resistance. These findings identify CAF-mediated coordination of T cell function as a critical determinant of heterogeneous immune checkpoint inhibitor responses and establish tumor assembloids as a platform for studying tumor microenvironment biology and personalized immunotherapy.
items.why_notable: This work is attracting attention because tumour assembloids that replicate the complex cellular environment of human renal cell carcinoma—including cancer cells, cancer-associated fibroblasts, and immune cells—have revealed a key pathway underlying variable responses to therapy. The model offers a more physiologically relevant platform for uncovering mechanisms of treatment resistance in kidney cancer.
items.citation: Eunjee Kim, 강민용, Jang Hee Han et al.. Tumour assembloids recapitulate tumour–CAF–T cell crosstalk in renal cancer. Nature. 2026

items.title: MCT1-dependent mitochondrial lactate import sustains cardiac metabolism
items.summary: The paper investigated how lactate, the highest turnover circulating metabolite in mammals, is metabolized in the heart, challenging the traditional view that lactate must first be converted to pyruvate in the cytosol before entering mitochondria for oxidation. Using stable isotope tracing in mice with genetic deletion of the mitochondrial pyruvate carrier, the researchers demonstrated that lactate can be imported directly into cardiac mitochondria and oxidized there independently of the canonical cytosolic pathway. This mitochondrial lactate import was found to depend on the monocarboxylate transporter MCT1, and mitochondria lacking MCT1 showed a specific defect in lactate but not pyruvate metabolism. The study further showed that mitochondrial lactate oxidation by mitochondrial lactate dehydrogenase functions as an electron shuttle capable of supporting respiration even when the TCA cycle is disrupted. Animals with cardiac-specific loss of MCT1 rapidly developed heart failure under stress, establishing that direct mitochondrial lactate import is essential for sustaining cardiac energetics and maintaining heart structure and function.
items.why_notable: This work is attracting attention because it reveals an alternative route by which the heart maintains energy production when the canonical mitochondrial pyruvate carrier is absent, with mitochondrial MCT1 and LDHB together shuttling lactate directly into mitochondria to sustain cardiac metabolism and prevent heart failure under stress.
items.citation: Ahmad A. Cluntun, Joseph R. Visker, Jesse N. Velasco‐Silva et al.. MCT1-dependent mitochondrial lactate import sustains cardiac metabolism. Nature. 2026

items.title: Eukaryotes’ closest relatives are internally simple syntrophic peptidotrophic archaea
items.summary: This paper investigated the biology of archaea closely related to the first eukaryotic common ancestor (FECA) by isolating and culturing two strains belonging to the order Hodarchaeales, which are members of the Promethearchaeota (formerly Asgard archaea), the archaeal group most closely related to eukaryotes. The researchers successfully grew these strains in defined co- and tri-cultures with methanogenic partners, enabling detailed physiological and genomic characterization. The isolated strains are obligately anaerobic, syntrophic, peptide-degrading, mesophilic archaea with simple internal cell structures that produce membrane protrusions and vesicles, and they prioritize cell construction over division rather than following typical prokaryotic growth patterns. Although one strain carries genes associated with aerobic lifestyles, it lacks complete aerobic respiration pathways and can only survive microaerobic conditions when aerobic partners are present, suggesting these genes function in oxygen detoxification. Taken together, the physiological, genomic, and phylogenetic evidence indicates that FECA was a simple-celled, anaerobic, syntrophic archaeon with limited aerotolerance, implying that the evolutionary transition from archaea to eukaryotes involved dramatic changes in both cellular complexity and the capacity for aerobic metabolism.
items.why_notable: This work is attracting attention because cultivated representatives of the archaeal lineage most closely related to eukaryotes reveal that these organisms are internally simple, syntrophic, and anaerobic, providing direct biological insight into the nature of the archaeal partner at the root of eukaryotic origins. The findings suggest that physical symbiosis and dependence on peptide-based nutrition are conserved features across this broader archaeal group, with major implications for understanding how complex eukaryotic cells evolved.
items.citation: Hiroyuki Imachi, Masaru Konishi Nobu, Shun’ichi Ishii et al.. Eukaryotes’ closest relatives are internally simple syntrophic peptidotrophic archaea. Nature. 2026

The result validates the concept of altermagnetism as a distinct and potentially useful magnetic phase for spintronic applications.

items.title: A single-molecule spin–photon interface
items.summary: This paper investigated whether a synthetically designed molecular system could serve as a robust spin–photon interface for quantum networking applications, a role previously dominated by solid-state atomic defects such as color centers in diamond. The researchers embedded a triplet ground-state carbene molecule into a structurally matched host crystal and characterized its optical and spin properties down to the single-molecule level. The system demonstrated narrow zero-phonon lines, spectral stability sustained over extended periods, spin-selective optical transitions, and single-molecule optically detected magnetic resonance. Coherent spin control achieved millisecond-scale coherence times under dynamical decoupling and tens-of-milliseconds spin relaxation at cryogenic temperatures. These findings establish that molecularly engineered qubits can simultaneously meet the demands of bright fluorescence, spectral stability, and long spin lifetimes, positioning bottom-up chemical design as a viable route to single-emitter quantum optical platforms.
items.why_notable: This work draws attention because it demonstrates that a single molecule can serve as a viable spin–photon interface with remarkably long coherence times, offering a chemically engineered route to molecular qubits suitable for quantum networking applications.
items.citation: Simon Roggors, Thomas Unden, Anna Aubele et al.. A single-molecule spin–photon interface. Nature. 2026

items.title: Spatial and sectoral water demand assessment for the African continent
items.summary: This paper investigated water demand across the African continent, examining how much water different economic and social sectors require and where those demands are concentrated spatially. The researchers integrated heterogeneous datasets and modelling approaches to generate harmonized estimates of water demand for the year 2020 across six sectors—municipalities, irrigation, livestock, manufacturing, electricity generation, and mining—at high spatial resolution. They found that irrigation dominates total continental water demand, followed by municipalities and electricity, with the dominant sector varying considerably by region and river basin in ways that reflect broader geographical and socioeconomic patterns. A notable finding is that in parts of northern and southern Africa estimated demand exceeds available water, while in other regions physical water availability is sufficient yet access to piped drinking water remains limited, demonstrating that scarcity and insecurity are not synonymous. The authors caution that their estimates represent harmonized approximations rather than observed water use, and that local-scale results should be interpreted carefully given underlying data uncertainties.
items.why_notable: This work is drawing attention because it provides a continent-wide assessment of water demand across multiple sectors, revealing that in certain regions water demand already surpasses available supply — a finding with significant implications for resource management and policy across Africa.

items.title: Alzheimer’s disease genetics converges on microglial and neuronal dysregulation
items.summary: This paper conducted a large-scale multi-ancestry genome-wide association study of Alzheimer's disease to identify genetic variants and biological pathways underlying the condition. By analyzing data from hundreds of thousands of cases, proxy cases, and controls drawn from diverse ancestries, the researchers identified numerous genomic loci associated with Alzheimer's disease risk, nearly half of which were previously unreported. They prioritized new risk genes and potential drug targets, and found that genes upregulated in microglia and downregulated in neurons in affected individuals were enriched for disease-associated genetic risk, pointing to microglial and neuronal dysregulation as central mechanisms. The study also substantially revised the estimated heritability attributable to common variants upward compared with prior estimates, suggesting that the genetic contribution to Alzheimer's disease has been considerably underestimated. These findings advance understanding of the molecular and cellular basis of Alzheimer's disease and highlight specific targets for future therapeutic development.
items.why_notable: This work is drawing attention because it identifies new genetic risk loci and potential drug targets for Alzheimer's disease while revealing that common genetic variants contribute more to the disease than previously thought. By implicating microglia and neurons as key players, it also helps clarify the biological pathways through which genetic risk operates.
authors: Mount Sinai Million Health Discoveries Program
items.citation: Emil Uffelmann, Douglas P. Wightman, Shahram Bahrami et al.. Alzheimer’s disease genetics converges on microglial and neuronal dysregulation. Nature. 2026

items.title: Pharmacological inhibition of METTL1 as a therapy against solid and blood cancers
items.summary: The paper investigated whether pharmacological inhibition of METTL1, an enzyme responsible for N7-methylguanosine modification of tRNAs, could serve as an anti-cancer therapeutic strategy. The researchers developed STM9005, a highly selective and potent first-in-class small molecule inhibitor of METTL1, and tested it across a range of cancer cell models including leukaemia, melanoma, pancreatic carcinoma, oesophageal cancer, and small cell lung carcinoma, as well as in multiple mouse cancer models in vivo. Treatment with STM9005 blocked cancer cell growth, induced differentiation changes, and dysregulated cell cycle progression, with these effects linked to a selective reduction in m7G modification on a subset of tRNAs and consequent impairment of oncogenic mRNA translation. In vivo, pharmacological inhibition of METTL1 suppressed tumour growth and prolonged survival across mouse models of different tissue origins. The findings establish proof of concept that targeting tRNA methylation represents a viable and promising anti-cancer therapeutic avenue.
items.why_notable: This work is attracting attention because it demonstrates that pharmacologically blocking METTL1, an enzyme responsible for a specific RNA modification, suppresses tumor growth and markedly extends survival across multiple cancer types in animal models, suggesting its potential as a broad anticancer therapeutic strategy.
items.citation: Eliza Yankova, Alexandra Sapetschnig, Beth Ann Thomas et al.. Pharmacological inhibition of METTL1 as a therapy against solid and blood cancers. Nature. 2026

items.title: SWI/SNF complexes shape 3D chromatin architecture through CTCF and cohesin
items.summary: This paper investigated how SWI/SNF chromatin remodeling complexes, specifically the canonical BAF (cBAF) subcomplex, influence three-dimensional genome organization. Using pharmacological inhibition and genetic deletion of ARID1A across multiple mammalian cell types and tissues, the researchers disrupted cBAF function and examined the resulting changes in chromatin accessibility, protein occupancy, and genome architecture. They found that cBAF loss consistently increased chromatin accessibility at CTCF-binding sites, leading to greater CTCF and cohesin occupancy and a reorganization of topologically associating domains into smaller insulated units, with long-range enhancer-promoter contacts replaced by shorter promoter-proximal loops. Mechanistically, the study revealed an antagonistic relationship between cBAF and CTCF-cohesin, mediated in part by a switch to PBAF recruitment at CTCF-enriched sites following cBAF depletion, as CTCF was found to interact directly with assembled PBAF. In vivo deletion of Arid1a in mouse cells produced a proliferative cellular phenotype that was fully reversed by deletion of either Ctcf or Pbrm1, establishing opposing functional roles for cBAF and the CTCF-PBAF axis in regulating genome organization and cell behavior.
items.why_notable: This work is attracting attention because it reveals that loss of a major chromatin-remodeling complex leads to widespread changes in the binding of key architectural proteins, fundamentally rewiring the three-dimensional organization of the genome and transcriptional programs. The findings establish a previously unappreciated link between chromatin remodeling and higher-order genome structure.
items.citation: Sonia M. Debek, Cem Meydan, Christopher R. Chin et al.. SWI/SNF complexes shape 3D chromatin architecture through CTCF and cohesin. Nature. 2026

items.title: Comprehensive sequence analysis reveals the vast β-lactam resistome
items.summary: This study investigated the global distribution of β-lactamase antibiotic resistance genes across diverse microbial taxa and environmental ecosystems, addressing limitations in scalability and taxonomic resolution that have hampered previous analyses. The researchers conducted a comprehensive sequence analysis to identify β-lactamases spanning all five enzyme classes across publicly available genomic and metagenomic data, producing a taxonomy-environment map of their occurrence. They discovered β-lactamases to be remarkably widespread, approaching the abundance of an essential housekeeping gene across environments, with particularly strong enrichment in wastewater and plant-associated samples. The enrichment in plant environments suggests these settings as ancient battlegrounds where an evolutionary arms race between β-lactam-producing and β-lactam-resistant bacteria has unfolded over millions of years. The study also traces the origins of clinically relevant β-lactamases primarily to Gamma-Proteobacteria and extends known reservoirs of these genes beyond wastewater to include plant, terrestrial, and aquatic environments.
items.citation: Sevan Gholipour, John Z. Chen, Dong‐Kyu Lee et al.. Comprehensive sequence analysis reveals the vast β-lactam resistome. Microbiome. 2026

items.title: Aircraft and Airport Wastewater Surveillance for Public Health Preparedness Demands an Integrated and Sustainable Approach.
items.summary: This review examined the use of wastewater surveillance collected from aircraft lavatories and airport infrastructure as a public health tool for detecting and monitoring infectious pathogens among traveling populations. The authors conducted a structured narrative review synthesizing existing evidence on the scientific, methodological, and interpretive dimensions of this surveillance approach, with particular attention to the factors that govern signal detectability and validity. The strongest evidence base concerns detection and variant monitoring of the virus responsible for the COVID-19 pandemic, though the authors note that signals are shaped by numerous variables including pathogen shedding dynamics, flight duration, sampling matrix, and assay sensitivity. They caution that wastewater signals are aggregate and population-level in nature and cannot be attributed to individual travelers, specific flights, or particular countries of origin. The review concludes that while aviation wastewater surveillance holds promise as an early-warning and situational-awareness tool, its broader extension to multiple pathogens and antimicrobial resistance markers requires pathogen-specific validation, clearer interpretive frameworks, and integration with complementary surveillance systems.
items.citation: Vaidya SR, Pandey PG, Giri S et al.. Aircraft and Airport Wastewater Surveillance for Public Health Preparedness Demands an Integrated and Sustainable Approach.. Viruses. 2026

items.title: From Sewers to Surveillance: Monitoring Salmonella Through Wastewater.
items.summary: Wastewater surveillance offers a population-level window into infectious disease burden that can capture cases missed by clinical reporting, including asymptomatic and unreported infections. This study developed and validated methods for detecting Salmonella in wastewater, combining sample concentration via PEG precipitation, magnetic bead-based nucleic acid extraction, and quantitative PCR. When deployed across a statewide surveillance network, the approach revealed seasonal transmission patterns and detected outbreak activity that passive clinical surveillance had failed to identify. Notably, wastewater signals preceded clinical case reports by approximately one week, demonstrating an early-warning advantage. The authors conclude that despite limitations such as low pathogen concentrations and an inability to resolve serovars, integrating wastewater surveillance with traditional public health systems substantially improves the detection and understanding of Salmonella dynamics.
items.citation: Kuhn KG, Shelton K, Rimal B et al.. From Sewers to Surveillance: Monitoring Salmonella Through Wastewater.. Methods in molecular biology (Clifton, N.J.). 2027
