items.title: Machine learning-enabled wastewater-based surveillance for emerging pathogen detection and monitoring: current applications, challenges, and future prospects.
items.summary: This review examined the use of machine learning to enhance wastewater-based surveillance as a public health tool for detecting and monitoring emerging pathogens. The authors conducted a narrative review of the published literature, classifying studies by the type of analytical approach used—ranging from classical statistical models through deep learning and hybrid mechanistic methods—and by the specific surveillance task addressed, such as forecasting, anomaly detection, and data harmonization. They found that the evidence base is heavily dominated by studies focused on SARS-CoV-2, that demonstrated early-warning capability came predominantly from simpler statistical methods rather than more complex machine learning approaches, and that reported performance varied substantially depending on context. Key barriers identified include sampling variability, laboratory inconsistencies, population-dependent biases, and the high-dimensional complexity of wastewater molecular data, all of which limit generalizability and validation. The authors call for standardized collaborative frameworks, multimodal data integration, mechanistic and uncertainty-aware modelling, and greater attention to governance and public acceptability to advance the field beyond its current largely proof-of-concept stage.
items.citation: Song A, Jia P, Luo J et al.. Machine learning-enabled wastewater-based surveillance for emerging pathogen detection and monitoring: current applications, challenges, and future prospects.. Emerging microbes & infections. 2026

items.title: Molecular Public Health for Infectious Disease Prevention and Control.
items.summary: This narrative review defines and examines "molecular public health" as an end-to-end operational framework that links molecular evidence to population-level decisions, interventions, and evaluation, distinguishing it from the broader field of molecular epidemiology. The authors integrate a wide range of technologies—including pathogen genomics, metagenomics, wastewater surveillance, One Health monitoring, antimicrobial resistance genomics, multi-omics, and artificial intelligence—within a progression from detection and interpretation through prediction, intervention, and feedback. The review finds that implementation maturity is uneven: established approaches such as targeted PCR, short-read pathogen genomics, and bioinformatics-supported outbreak investigation are well embedded in defined use cases, while pathogen-agnostic metagenomics, multi-omics, and AI-enabled decision support remain context-dependent or emerging. Actionability is assessed through criteria including analytical validity, epidemiological interpretability, sample-to-decision time relative to the intervention window, and measurable post-intervention outcomes. The authors identify persistent barriers—among them sampling bias, uneven global capacity, incomplete metadata, poor standardization, and unclear trigger thresholds—and argue that the central criterion for the field should be whether molecular information demonstrably improves infectious disease prevention and control.
items.citation: Kimura H, Kimura R, Mizukoshi F et al.. Molecular Public Health for Infectious Disease Prevention and Control.. Microorganisms. 2026

items.title: Multimodal genomic surveillance for respiratory pathogens at four U.S. international airports: A comparison of air, wastewater, clinical, and national surveillance data.
items.summary: This study evaluated air sampling as a surveillance tool for respiratory pathogens at major U.S. international airports, comparing its performance against aviation wastewater, traveler nasal swabs, and national clinical data. Over a roughly ten-month period, air samples from congregate areas at four airports were analyzed using PCR and two sequencing approaches, including targeted amplicon and targeted enrichment sequencing. SARS-CoV-2 was detected in nearly all air samples while influenza A was detected less frequently, and influenza A positivity showed strong correlations with other surveillance modalities whereas SARS-CoV-2 measurements did not correlate well across data streams. Sequencing of air samples identified contemporaneous viral lineages and recovered high-quality genomes for multiple respiratory viruses including SARS-CoV-2, influenza, bocavirus, and seasonal coronaviruses, collectively detecting dozens of viral species. The authors conclude that air sampling can serve as a complementary tool to wastewater surveillance at ports of entry, though its utility varies depending on the pathogen and the comparison surveillance modality.
items.citation: Gratalo D, Friedman CR, Morley VJ et al.. Multimodal genomic surveillance for respiratory pathogens at four U.S. international airports: A comparison of air, wastewater, clinical, and national surveillance data.. PLOS global public health. 2026

items.title: Inferring variant-specific effective reproduction numbers from combined case and sequencing data
items.summary: This paper addresses the challenge of accurately estimating the transmission rates of co-circulating SARS-CoV-2 variants using richer epidemiological data than sequence frequencies alone. The authors developed a method that jointly analyzes confirmed case counts and genetic sequencing data to infer variant-specific effective reproduction numbers alongside variant frequencies across states in the United States over more than a year of the pandemic. Their approach allows structured relationships between effective reproduction numbers to be estimated across time series, including fixed variant-specific growth advantages that can be compared across geographic locations. Applying this framework to variants of concern and interest, they demonstrated that combining case and sequencing data captures epidemiological dynamics that sequence proportions alone cannot reveal. The method produces consistent estimates of growth advantages for specific variants across different locations, offering a more complete picture of variant transmission behavior than frequency-based approaches.
items.citation: Marlin D Figgins, Trevor Bedford. Inferring variant-specific effective reproduction numbers from combined case and sequencing data. eLife. 2026

items.title: Beyond the visible: metal-ion-doped inorganic UV phosphors for advanced photonics
items.summary: This review paper examines inorganic ultraviolet luminescent materials doped with metal ions, including rare-earth and heavy main-group metal ions, which display distinctive electronic transitions, excellent photostability, and tunable emission properties. The authors systematically survey three major luminescence modes — persistent luminescence, upconversion luminescence, and mechanoluminescence — covering their underlying mechanisms, recent advances, and material design strategies. The review is further organized by spectral classification and applies the principle that performance requirements should guide application selection. These UV phosphors are highlighted as promising candidates for optoelectronics, environmental remediation, and biomedical uses. The paper concludes by identifying key outstanding challenges and future research directions to guide continued development of inorganic UV luminescent materials.
items.citation: Yu Zhang, Yanjie Liang, Feng Liu et al.. Beyond the visible: metal-ion-doped inorganic UV phosphors for advanced photonics. Light Science & Applications. 2026

items.title: Quantitative Microbial Risk Assessment of Human H5N1 Infection From Consumption of Fluid Cow's Milk
items.summary: This study used quantitative microbial risk assessment to evaluate the public health threat posed by the H5N1 influenza strain that spilled over into dairy cattle, specifically examining the risk of human infection through consumption of fluid cow's milk. Researchers developed stochastic farm-to-table models parameterized with data emerging from the ongoing outbreak to estimate infection probabilities per serving of pasteurized and raw milk and to evaluate potential risk-reduction interventions. The analysis found that pasteurized milk carries an essentially negligible infection risk, while raw milk purchased at farm stores or retail outlets carries substantially higher, though still relatively low, per-serving infection probabilities. Scenario analyses identified bulk tank milk testing using quantitative real-time reverse transcriptase PCR as an effective intervention for reducing risk associated with raw milk consumption. The study also highlights critical knowledge gaps regarding human dose-response relationships for H5N1 ingestion and raw milk consumption patterns, underscoring the need for further research and the value of mechanistic epidemiologic models during foodborne disease outbreaks.
items.citation: Katherine J Koebel, Ece Bulut, Samuel David Alcaine et al.. Quantitative Microbial Risk Assessment of Human H5N1 Infection From Consumption of Fluid Cow's Milk. Risk Analysis. 2026

items.title: Antimicrobial resistance in aquaculture an overview of current status and possible solutions to the issue
items.summary: This review paper examines the problem of antimicrobial resistance arising from antibiotic use in aquaculture, tracing how resistance develops and spreads through aquatic environments. The authors survey global patterns of antibiotic use across aquaculture species and explore the ecological and genetic mechanisms driving resistance, including horizontal gene transfer, biofilm formation, and the persistence of antibiotic resistance genes in sediments and water bodies. The review also assesses existing national and international regulatory frameworks, identifying significant gaps in monitoring, enforcement, and cross-country coordination. A range of alternative strategies are evaluated, encompassing vaccines, probiotics, phage therapy, plant antimicrobials, nanotechnology, and precision aquaculture, alongside molecular surveillance tools such as metagenomics and quantitative PCR for tracking resistance. The authors conclude by advocating a One Health approach that integrates veterinary, environmental, and public health sectors, and call for policy harmonization, capacity building, and targeted research investment to promote sustainable, antibiotic-responsible aquaculture.
items.citation: Shafiya Mushtaq, Tasaduq Hussain Shah, Nahida Quyoom et al.. Antimicrobial resistance in aquaculture an overview of current status and possible solutions to the issue. Discover Environment. 2026

items.title: Pathogenicity and virulence of Candida auris
items.summary: This paper provides a comprehensive review of *Candida auris*, an emerging multidrug-resistant fungal pathogen responsible for infections with high morbidity and mortality in healthcare settings. The authors examine both host and pathogen factors that govern the organism's distinctive capacity to colonize human skin, which facilitates efficient person-to-person transmission and promotes outbreaks particularly in nursing homes caring for elderly patients. A central concern addressed is the pathogen's widespread resistance to all major antifungal drug classes—azoles, polyenes, and echinocandins—rendering some infections effectively untreatable and driving very high mortality even when therapy is administered. The review also discusses the challenges associated with preventing dissemination of the organism and managing established invasive infections.
items.citation: Trinh Phan-Canh, Saskia Seiser, Manju Chauhan et al.. Pathogenicity and virulence of Candida auris. Virulence. 2026

items.title: Dittany: Contribution-Guided Repair Framework for MAS Applications
items.summary: The paper investigates the problem of repairing failed or incomplete executions in large language model-based multi-agent system applications, where useful intermediate work may be produced even when overall task requirements go unmet. The authors developed Dittany, a runtime repair framework that constructs a contribution graph by deriving expected contributions and acceptance conditions from task requirements and method specifications, using this structure to identify which results remain valid and which work still needs to be done. When failures are detected, the framework applies either action-level correction—when sufficient valid inputs are available—or graph-level recovery to revise missing prerequisites, in both cases preserving already-validated contributions and verifying repaired outputs before they are used downstream. Evaluated across a large set of applications spanning multiple multi-agent frameworks and thousands of tasks, Dittany substantially outperforms both unassisted native execution and competing recovery baselines in task accuracy while incurring only modest additional token costs compared to those baselines. Ablation studies confirm that combining both repair scopes yields better accuracy and lower token consumption than using graph-level repair alone.
items.citation: Hanqi Sun, Yuchen Shao, Hanyi Si et al.. Dittany: Contribution-Guided Repair Framework for MAS Applications. arXiv. 2026

items.title: SATFRONT: Detecting Atmospheric Fronts with Satellite Data using Machine Learning
items.summary: This paper addresses the challenge of automatically identifying atmospheric fronts, which are key drivers of high-impact weather in the mid-latitudes but have traditionally been identified through subjective manual analysis. The authors developed SATFRONT, a machine learning framework that detects cold, warm, and occluded fronts over Europe using geostationary satellite observations, optionally supplemented by reanalysis data, and trained it on frontal analyses from multiple European meteorological services. Using satellite data alone, the model performs within the range of inter-agency agreement among meteorological services and substantially outperforms an existing operational rule-based satellite-based detector, with performance improving further when reanalysis data is incorporated. The reanalysis input particularly improves the spatial placement of individual fronts, though its influence on annual spatial distributions varies by front type. These findings demonstrate that automated, high-temporal-frequency frontal detection directly from satellite observations is feasible, opening the door to timelier frontal analyses for operational meteorology.
items.citation: Ioannis Dravilas, Miruna Stoicescu, Roope Tervo et al.. SATFRONT: Detecting Atmospheric Fronts with Satellite Data using Machine Learning. arXiv. 2026

items.title: Soft X-Ray Detection Down to the Nitrogen K-Edge Using a Pixelated iLGAD Sensor
items.summary: The paper investigates the use of inverse low-gain avalanche diode sensors with thin entrance windows as a solution for extending hybrid pixel detector technology into the soft X-ray regime, where achieving high quantum efficiency and adequate signal-to-noise ratios at low photon energies has remained a major challenge. Two gain layer designs — a standard gain layer and a shallow gain layer — were fabricated and tested, with their spectral responses characterized as a function of photon energy and operating temperature. The sensors demonstrated single-photon resolution down to energies below the Nitrogen K-edge with a signal-to-noise ratio sufficient for practical use. A notable double-peak feature observed in the energy spectra was attributed to the dependence of charge multiplication on photon absorption depth, and a phenomenological spectral fitting model was developed to extract key device parameters such as the effective layer thicknesses. These results advance understanding of charge multiplication mechanisms in such sensors and establish a path toward large-area, high-frame-rate hybrid pixel detectors suitable for soft X-ray applications including ptychography, spectroscopy, and resonant scattering at synchrotron and free-electron laser facilities.
items.citation: Shuqi Li, Anna Bergamaschi, Ashish Bisht et al.. Soft X-Ray Detection Down to the Nitrogen K-Edge Using a Pixelated iLGAD Sensor. arXiv. 2026

items.title: Tests of equivalence principle violation in doubly coupled dark energy
items.summary: This paper investigates coupled dark energy models in which dark matter, but not baryons, couples to a scalar field, thereby violating the weak equivalence principle. The authors generalize this framework by introducing an additional nonminimal coupling between the scalar field and gravity, creating what they call "doubly coupled dark energy," and they construct a parameter to quantify equivalence principle violation on cosmological scales in a model-independent manner. Using forecasts for current and future spectroscopic galaxy surveys, they assess how well the coupling strengths can be constrained, allowing the initial power spectrum shape and galaxy bias to vary freely across multiple bins. Among the surveys considered, including DESI, Euclid, and SKA Phase 2, the latter is predicted to provide the tightest constraints on the coupling strength, though these constraints weaken when both couplings are varied simultaneously and improve with larger galaxy samples.
items.citation: Yannick Kegel, Ziyang Zheng, Luca Amendola. Tests of equivalence principle violation in doubly coupled dark energy. arXiv. 2026

items.title: Proof-Carrying Evolution: Black-Box Search, White-Box Flight
items.summary: This paper investigates whether language models can assist in designing controllers that come with formal mathematical certificates verifying their behavioral properties, a framework the authors call proof-carrying evolution. In this approach, a language model proposes both a controller and its certificate simultaneously, with certificate checks guiding selection so that only formally verified candidates are deployed, while the language model itself plays no role after design. The method was tested on three control problems of varying complexity, including spacecraft docking, pursuit of a maneuvering target, and attitude control on a nonlinear manifold, comparing language models against classical search and synthesis methods under controlled experimental conditions. Results showed that the strongest language models outperformed classical baselines on linear problems, though a classical optimizer augmented with certificate selection largely closed this performance gap, and no model consistently beat a standard evolutionary algorithm on the nonlinear problem. A key finding was that retaining certified candidates during search was essential, as runs enforcing this rule reliably produced new certified designs while runs without it produced none, underscoring that the certification mechanism rather than the language model alone drives the framework's reliability.
items.citation: Amit Jain, Sergio Sanchez-Hurtado, Victor Rodriguez-Fernandez et al.. Proof-Carrying Evolution: Black-Box Search, White-Box Flight. arXiv. 2026

items.title: A richness-sensitive Acoustic Biodiversity Index from species-level detections: classifier benchmarking, false-positive control and validation against standard soundscape indices in an African savanna and an urban zoo
items.summary: The paper revised and tested an Acoustic Biodiversity Index built from species-level detections rather than raw sound energy distributions, addressing a known weakness of conventional acoustic indices in tracking species richness. The authors benchmarked four classifier approaches on a labelled tropical bird call dataset and applied the best-performing combination to passive acoustic recordings from a riverine savanna in Zimbabwe and multiple habitat types at a zoo in Abu Dhabi. A key methodological contribution was the implementation of explicit false-positive control through location and season filtering, which removed hundreds of high-confidence but implausible detections, and effort standardisation via diel-matched rarefaction. The revised index correlated strongly with observed species richness across recorded hours, substantially outperforming six standard soundscape indices, the best of which showed only a weak correlation. The authors conclude that species-level acoustic indices with transparent false-positive control and a declared regional reference pool offer more interpretable and ecologically meaningful biodiversity indicators than energy-based approaches, while also noting that the temporal stability component penalises natural diel activity cycles.
items.citation: Muhammad Saeed, Dmitry Mikhaylov, Mohamed H. Alhosani et al.. A richness-sensitive Acoustic Biodiversity Index from species-level detections: classifier benchmarking, false-positive control and validation against standard soundscape indices in an African savanna and an urban zoo. arXiv. 2026

items.title: Rapid and Sensitive Detection of <i>Schistosoma mansoni</i> in the Intermediate Snail Hosts Using Loop-Mediated Isothermal Amplification (LAMP) Diagnostics.
items.summary: The study addressed the need for improved detection of *Schistosoma mansoni* infection in its intermediate snail hosts, which is critical for schistosomiasis control but hampered by the low sensitivity of conventional parasitological methods. Researchers developed a novel loop-mediated isothermal amplification assay targeting the mitochondrial NADH dehydrogenase subunit 1 gene of *S. mansoni*, optimized it for a single temperature and short reaction time, and evaluated its performance against microscopy, conventional PCR, and real-time PCR using both laboratory-infected snails and field-collected samples from two endemic countries. In laboratory settings, the assay achieved complete specificity and sensitivity superior to microscopy, while field testing revealed it detected a higher proportion of infected snails than conventional PCR and identified infections entirely missed by parasitological examination. The authors conclude that this LAMP assay is a sensitive, specific, and practically deployable diagnostic tool suitable for routine snail surveillance and early detection of shifts in schistosomiasis transmission.
items.citation: Li HM, Qin ZQ, Lv S et al.. Rapid and Sensitive Detection of <i>Schistosoma mansoni</i> in the Intermediate Snail Hosts Using Loop-Mediated Isothermal Amplification (LAMP) Diagnostics.. Tropical medicine and infectious disease. 2026

items.title: Point of Care Testing and Recombinase Polymerase Amplification.

items.title: CRISPR/Cas-Based Molecular Diagnostics for Intestinal Parasites: From Proof-of-Concept to Point-of-Care Testing.
items.summary: This review examines the application of CRISPR/Cas-based diagnostic systems for detecting intestinal and foodborne parasitic infections, which pose a persistent public health burden especially in resource-limited settings where conventional diagnostic tools face significant constraints. The authors surveyed published assays targeting key parasites including *Giardia duodenalis*, *Cryptosporidium parvum*, *Clonorchis sinensis*, *Fasciola hepatica*, and *Schistosoma* species, focusing on how CRISPR effector proteins have been coupled with isothermal amplification methods to enable rapid detection. The platforms reviewed predominantly use Cas12a alongside recombinase-based amplification strategies, producing results within roughly one to one-and-a-half hours via fluorescence or lateral-flow readouts, and demonstrate high analytical sensitivity and specificity with reasonable concordance with established molecular methods. Nevertheless, the review identifies important limitations including dependence on nucleic acid extraction, small clinical validation cohorts, absence of standardized protocols, and false-negative results at low parasite burdens. The authors conclude that while CRISPR/Cas diagnostics represent a promising next-generation approach for point-of-care parasite detection, large-scale clinical validation and further workflow optimization are necessary before these platforms can be broadly implemented in routine or field settings.
items.citation: Alsaady IM. CRISPR/Cas-Based Molecular Diagnostics for Intestinal Parasites: From Proof-of-Concept to Point-of-Care Testing.. Diagnostics (Basel, Switzerland). 2026

items.title: Hantavirus Emergence in a Changing World: Virology, Pathogenesis, Surveillance, and One Health Preparedness
items.summary: This review examines hantaviruses as emerging rodent-borne pathogens responsible for serious diseases including hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome and hantavirus cardiopulmonary syndrome, with attention to the environmental and ecological factors driving their spread. The authors synthesize current knowledge across virology, epidemiology, pathogenesis, clinical presentation, diagnostics, and prevention strategies. Particular focus is placed on how climate change, urbanization, and land-use transformation alter rodent reservoir dynamics and increase the risk of spillover to humans, as well as on surveillance and diagnostic gaps in tropical and Caribbean regions where the burden may be underestimated. The review also discusses advances in molecular diagnostics, genomic surveillance, vaccine development, monoclonal antibody therapies, and climate-based early warning systems. The authors conclude that integrated One Health surveillance combining human, animal, and environmental monitoring, alongside strengthened laboratory capacity and regional collaboration, is essential for improving outbreak preparedness and reducing the global burden of hantavirus disease.
items.citation: Maria E. Ramos‐Niño, Nicolette Chiem, Prakash V. A. K. Ramdass. Hantavirus Emergence in a Changing World: Virology, Pathogenesis, Surveillance, and One Health Preparedness. Microorganisms. 2026

items.title: The analysis of natural gemstones and their synthetic counterparts using analytical spectroscopy methods
items.summary: This study examined whether Raman spectroscopy could reliably distinguish natural gemstones from their laboratory-grown synthetic counterparts across four major commercial gems: ruby, sapphire, emerald, and spinel. The researchers evaluated both a laboratory Raman spectrometer equipped with two laser wavelengths and a portable Raman system, applying these tools to identify gemstones produced by different manufacturing methods without requiring sample preparation or causing damage to the specimens. The laboratory instrument successfully differentiated natural from synthetic gemstones and could even determine geographic origin among stones of the same color, though emerald analysis required the shorter-wavelength laser exclusively. The portable system was capable of distinguishing between different stone types but lacked the sensitivity needed to discriminate natural from synthetic gems. Overall, the findings support Raman spectroscopy as a reliable and practical analytical approach for gemological identification, with laboratory-grade instruments offering greater discriminatory power than portable alternatives.
items.citation: Raabell Shah. The analysis of natural gemstones and their synthetic counterparts using analytical spectroscopy methods. Research Output (Edinburgh Napier University). 2026

items.title: Viral metagenomics of synanthropic urban bats: A surveillance strategy for uncovering potentially zoonotic viruses
items.summary: Bats are known reservoirs for numerous viruses capable of zoonotic spillover, yet systematic surveillance of bat-borne viral diversity remains limited, particularly in low- and middle-income countries. This study developed a metagenomics-based surveillance framework that capitalizes on an existing rabies passive surveillance program in Brazil, using an algorithmic selection strategy to choose representative bat specimens for nanopore sequencing of paired lung and intestine samples. Sequencing revealed viral contigs spanning multiple families of public health relevance, including coronaviruses, arenaviruses, and paramyxoviruses, and notably identified a previously unknown filovirus in bats from the Americas. These results demonstrate that repurposing existing animal surveillance infrastructure can efficiently uncover hidden viral diversity and enhance epidemic preparedness. The framework was further validated by a multisectoral One Health expert workshop as a scalable and cost-effective model suitable for national expansion and adaptation to low- and middle-income country settings.
items.citation: Juliana Amorim Conselheiro, Filipe Romero Rebello Moreira, Gisely Toledo Barone et al.. Viral metagenomics of synanthropic urban bats: A surveillance strategy for uncovering potentially zoonotic viruses. One Health. 2026

items.title: A Review on Artificial Intelligence Methods for Plant Disease and Pest Detection
items.summary: This review examines the application of artificial intelligence methods to plant disease and pest detection in agriculture, synthesizing existing research across a broad range of sensing modalities, learning paradigms, and deployment scales. The authors organize the literature by distinguishing between population-level pest monitoring, plant-centric visual inspection, and field-scale surveillance, as well as between post-symptomatic and pre-symptomatic detection approaches enabled by spectral imaging. A central focus is critical analysis of fundamental limitations, including data scarcity, domain shift, poor generalization under real field conditions, and the difficulty of separating biotic from abiotic stress signals. The review also addresses the conceptual gap between correlation-driven AI predictions and genuine causal understanding of disease, positioning AI as a decision-support complement to established diagnostic methods rather than a replacement. Looking forward, the authors identify multimodal sensor fusion, explainable AI, edge deployment for real-time monitoring, and foundation models for unified agricultural intelligence as key directions for advancing the field.
items.citation: Nikolaos Giakoumoglou, Dimitrios Kapetas, Kleanthis Marios Papadopoulos et al.. A Review on Artificial Intelligence Methods for Plant Disease and Pest Detection. AI and Precision Agriculture. 2026

items.citation: Zhang Zhen, Liu Shuhua, Ma Baihe et al.. Advances in rapid microbiological testing for animal diseases: A review. Journal of Microbiological Methods. 2026

items.title: Human Metapneumovirus (HMPV): Advances in Diagnosis, Molecular Epidemiology, and Clinical Impact of an Underrecognized Respiratory Virus
items.summary: Human metapneumovirus is a respiratory pathogen that disproportionately affects immunocompromised individuals, the elderly, and young children, though evidence now challenges the assumption that healthy adults are immune to serious disease. First identified in the early 2000s, the virus causes a spectrum of illness ranging from mild upper respiratory infections to severe pneumonia. This review synthesizes current literature on the epidemiology, molecular virology, and clinical characteristics of the virus, highlighting its substantial contribution to respiratory morbidity across populations. The authors emphasize that HMPV remains underrecognized and underappreciated as a public health threat, and they call for improved diagnostic capabilities and stronger public health measures to address this gap.
items.citation: ‏Helal F. Hetta, Rehab Ahmed, Abdul Haseeb et al.. Human Metapneumovirus (HMPV): Advances in Diagnosis, Molecular Epidemiology, and Clinical Impact of an Underrecognized Respiratory Virus. Diagnostics. 2026

items.title: Counting on Dummies: Privacy Amplification with Observable Counts and Truncated Batches
items.summary: This paper addresses two practical challenges that arise when deploying Differentially Private Stochastic Gradient Descent in real-world systems: the leakage of batch size information and the privacy degradation caused by truncating oversized batches. The authors identify that when batch sizes are observable—by a server, an aggregator, or through network traffic analysis—the standard privacy amplification guarantees of schemes like Poisson sampling and random allocation break down, and that truncating batches to a maximum size further compounds privacy loss. To address both issues simultaneously, they propose a mechanism that pads each batch with a random number of dummy data points, thereby obscuring the true batch size and preserving privacy guarantees even when truncation is applied. They provide a general analysis applicable to both Poisson sampling and random allocation, designed for efficient and tight privacy accounting, and show that the expected number of dummy points needed is asymptotically smaller than what direct privatization of batch sizes would require. Empirical results demonstrate that their mechanism achieves better privacy–efficiency tradeoffs for Poisson sampling with truncated batches compared to a recently proposed direct accounting approach.
items.citation: Vitaly Feldman, Audra McMillan, Kunal Talwar. Counting on Dummies: Privacy Amplification with Observable Counts and Truncated Batches. arXiv. 2026

items.title: Think in 360°: Benchmarking and Bootstrapping Panoramic Video Reasoning
items.summary: This paper addresses the challenge of understanding panoramic videos, where relevant information can appear in any direction and at any point in time, requiring models to integrate evidence across both the viewing sphere and temporal dimension. The authors introduce a manually annotated benchmark of one thousand questions across multiple categories to evaluate panoramic video comprehension, finding through testing of over a dozen models that cross-view tracking and sphere-time evidence integration are the most problematic capabilities. To address these weaknesses, they construct a reasoning dataset by converting verified panoramic observations and successful agentic explorations into tens of thousands of question-answer chains of thought grounded in real panoramic video. They then train a model called PanoVideoReasoner using a combination of panoramic chain-of-thought supervised fine-tuning and a self-distillation approach in which a teacher with access to verified perspective views guides student-generated reasoning trajectories. The resulting model substantially outperforms both its backbone and the previous state of the art on the new benchmark, with gains concentrated precisely in the spatial, cross-view, and temporal reasoning capabilities identified as weakest, demonstrating that grounded sphere-time supervision can meaningfully extend general video models to panoramic reasoning.
items.citation: Lidong Lu, Lidong Zou, Xinyi Mao et al.. Think in 360°: Benchmarking and Bootstrapping Panoramic Video Reasoning. arXiv. 2026

items.title: The Knowledge Layer Model (KLM): Evidence-Visible AI Output, Routing Diagnostics, and Negative Results
items.summary: This paper introduces the Knowledge Layer Model (KLM), an open specification designed to make the evidential basis of AI-generated outputs inspectable, including versioned epistemic assessments, evidence relations, and explicit representations of unknowns. The authors present a reference implementation called SEDIM within the Nage AI OS architecture, and report a series of internal empirical experiments intended to characterize system behavior across routing, retrieval, and diagnostic tasks. Results were notably mixed: while a historical routing benchmark showed high classification accuracy, a corrected two-source native-model test produced no successful answers, and two diagnostic methods both yielded discrimination performance far below the registered minimum threshold. A text-preservation fix improved gold-content retention from a majority of failures to complete success across tested cases, though the authors caution this measures text presence rather than answer quality. The paper is transparent about substantial limitations, including unverified historical data, a defective legacy scorer, and the absence of independent replication, explicitly distinguishing evidence visibility from correctness, security, or regulatory compliance.
items.citation: Omer Asim Ozturk, Cihan Aydiner. The Knowledge Layer Model (KLM): Evidence-Visible AI Output, Routing Diagnostics, and Negative Results. arXiv. 2026

items.title: When Does Jacobian Fine-Tuning Stabilize Neural PDE Emulators?
items.summary: This paper investigates when Jacobian-based fine-tuning methods improve the long-term stability of neural network emulators for chaotic partial differential equations. The core challenge is that these emulators are trained on single-step predictions but used autoregressively, causing errors to compound over time—though some error growth is physically inevitable in chaotic systems. The authors introduce a first-order decomposition that separates physical error amplification from amplification caused by the model's own dynamics, quantifying the latter as an "amplification ratio." Testing across numerous configurations spanning multiple PDEs, architectures, and model sizes, they find that Jacobian fine-tuning yields substantial error reduction only when the amplification ratio is sufficiently large, with negligible benefit when errors are already growing at physically determined rates. They also find that aligning the model's Jacobian with the solver's Jacobian along the model's own error direction outperforms random-direction approaches, while input-noise injection performs comparably to this targeted method.
items.citation: Shreeyam Bangera, Manya Gupta. When Does Jacobian Fine-Tuning Stabilize Neural PDE Emulators?. arXiv. 2026

items.title: Compound drop impacts on substrates of different temperatures
items.summary: This study investigated the impact dynamics of compound drops — drops consisting of a core fluid encased in a shell fluid — on substrates held at different temperatures. The researchers extended an existing parameter-free model, based on kinematic closure, to predict the maximum spreading diameter of both the core and shell components during isothermal impacts across various viscous fluid combinations. They then explored impacts on cold surfaces, exploiting the differing melting and freezing temperatures of the two constituent liquids to selectively freeze one or both fluids. By controlling which components solidify, they demonstrated that distinct frozen drop morphologies can be produced. The work thus advances both the theoretical modeling of compound drop spreading and the practical understanding of how thermal conditions can be used to engineer solidification patterns.
items.citation: Benjamin Gorin, Mete Abbot, Daniel Bonn et al.. Compound drop impacts on substrates of different temperatures. arXiv. 2026

items.title: The multiple origins of spurs in stellar streams: a challenge for dark matter diagnostics
items.summary: The paper investigated whether spurs observed along stellar streams can reliably serve as diagnostic signatures of dark matter subhalo interactions, as is commonly assumed. Using simulations, the authors modeled stream disruptions caused by three distinct mechanisms: dark matter subhalos, a galactic bar, and galaxy mergers. They found that all three processes produce morphologically similar spurs, with galaxy mergers being the most frequent cause in their simulations. The results demonstrate a significant degeneracy between baryonic and dark matter perturbers, meaning that spur morphology alone cannot identify the mechanism responsible for their formation or constrain the nature of dark matter.
items.citation: Claire Guillaume, Alicia Rivero, Titouan Le Guillois et al.. The multiple origins of spurs in stellar streams: a challenge for dark matter diagnostics. arXiv. 2026

items.title: Circulating calprotectin and S100A8/A9-related biomarkers for diagnosis and prognostic stratification in adult acute infection and sepsis: a systematic review and meta-analysis.
items.summary: This systematic review and meta-analysis examined whether circulating calprotectin and related S100A8/A9 biomarkers can accurately diagnose acute infection and sepsis or stratify prognosis in adult patients. The investigators searched major biomedical databases and trial registries, pooling data from over twenty independent cohorts using random-effects models and bivariate analyses, while assessing study quality with established diagnostic accuracy and evidence-grading tools. Across diagnostic outcomes, the pooled discriminatory performance was moderate for both sepsis and infection-related endpoints, and prognostic discrimination for mortality was similarly modest. Threshold-based analyses revealed variable sensitivity and specificity profiles depending on the clinical context, and paired comparisons with other biomarkers did not demonstrate clear superiority of calprotectin. The authors conclude that these biomarkers may serve as adjunctive indicators of host immune response in selected clinical contrasts, but the very low certainty of current evidence does not support their use as standalone diagnostic tools, their application with universal thresholds, or their replacement of established biomarkers and clinical judgment.
items.venue: Frontiers in cellular and infection microbiology
items.citation: Liao YS, Deng YP, Song JL et al.. Circulating calprotectin and S100A8/A9-related biomarkers for diagnosis and prognostic stratification in adult acute infection and sepsis: a systematic review and meta-analysis.. Frontiers in cellular and infection microbiology. 2026
